0.q: Which three sensory inputs does the brain integrate to maintain balance?
0.e: Postural control combines vestibular, visual and somatosensory (proprioceptive) input, integrated mainly in the vestibular nuclei and cerebellum.

0.q: How many vestibular sensory end-organs does each inner ear contain?
0.e: Three cristae (horizontal, anterior and posterior canals) plus two maculae (utricle and saccule) give five sensors per ear.

0.q: The semicircular canals primarily detect which stimulus?
o: Static head tilt relative to gravity
0.e: Canals sense angular (rotational) acceleration; the otolith organs sense linear acceleration and head tilt relative to gravity.

0.q: Primary vestibular afferents fire at about 90 spikes/s at rest. What is the main advantage of this resting discharge?
o: One afferent can signal rotation in both directions by rising or falling rate
It prevents fatigue of the hair cells
It makes the nerve insensitive to slow head movement
It is needed only to maintain hearing thresholds
0.e: A high tonic rate lets each afferent code excitation (rate up) and inhibition (rate down), giving the bidirectional push–pull signal the brainstem compares.

0.q: A patient with acute unilateral vestibular loss veers and falls toward the affected side when walking. Which output pathway chiefly maintains upright posture?
0.e: Vestibulospinal tracts drive antigravity muscles. An imbalance between the two sides produces veering or falling toward the lesioned ear.

1.q: Which structure in the ampulla is deflected by endolymph movement during head rotation?
1.e: The gelatinous cupula spans the ampulla. Endolymph lags behind the head (inertia), bending the cupula and the hair-cell bundles embedded in it.

1.q: A patient turns the head quickly to the right. What happens to horizontal canal afferent firing?
o: Both horizontal canals are excited equally
No change; only the otoliths respond
1.e: The canals work as push–pull pairs: rotation toward one side excites the ipsilateral horizontal canal and inhibits the contralateral one.

1.q: Which vertical canals form a coplanar push–pull pair?
1.e: The vertical canals pair diagonally across the head: left anterior–right posterior (LARP) and right anterior–left posterior (RALP).

1.q: According to Ewald's second law, which endolymph flow is excitatory in the horizontal canal?
o: Only flow toward the common crus
1.e: Horizontal canal: ampullopetal flow excites. Vertical canals: ampullofugal flow excites, because their hair-cell kinocilia are oriented the opposite way.

1.q: Why does a fast head impulse toward a lesioned ear reveal the deficit even though the healthy ear is intact?
o: The healthy ear is switched off during impulses
The otoliths block canal signals at high speed
The healthy ear's cupula becomes fixed
Inhibition of the healthy ear saturates as firing cannot fall below zero
1.e: Ewald's third law: excitation gives a larger response than inhibition. At high velocities the healthy ear's inhibitory response cuts off, so it cannot drive an adequate VOR.

2.q: Otoconia are composed mainly of which substance?
2.e: Otoconia are calcium carbonate crystals embedded in the otolithic membrane, giving it mass so gravity and linear acceleration shear the hair cells.

2.q: Which statement best describes the orientation of the maculae with the head upright?
o: Utricle roughly horizontal, saccule roughly vertical
Both lie vertically in the coronal plane
2.e: The utricular macula is roughly horizontal (sensing horizontal linear motion and tilt) and the saccular macula roughly vertical (sensing vertical acceleration).

2.q: What is the functional significance of the striola?
o: It is where otoconia are produced
It is the attachment site of the cupula
Hair-cell polarity reverses across it, so every direction of tilt is coded
2.e: Hair bundles are oppositely polarised on either side of the striola, so any direction of linear acceleration excites some hair cells and inhibits others.

2.q: A cVEMP recorded from the sternocleidomastoid primarily assesses which pathway?
o: Horizontal canal and superior vestibular nerve
2.e: cVEMP is an inhibitory potential in the ipsilateral SCM, driven by the saccule via the inferior vestibular nerve and vestibulospinal pathway.

2.q: A patient with right vestibular neuritis has an absent right oVEMP but a normal right cVEMP. Which nerve division is affected?
2.e: oVEMP (recorded under the contralateral eye, inferior oblique) reflects utricle and superior nerve function; a spared cVEMP means the inferior division is intact.

3.q: A rapid head turn to the right excites the right horizontal canal. Which nucleus is driven to move the LEFT eye outward?
3.e: The right vestibular nuclei excite the contralateral (left) abducens nucleus, which drives the left lateral rectus so the eyes rotate left, opposite to the head.

3.q: Which pathway links the abducens nucleus to the contralateral oculomotor nucleus for conjugate horizontal VOR?
3.e: Abducens interneurons project via the MLF to the opposite oculomotor (III) nucleus, which drives the medial rectus. A lesion here causes internuclear ophthalmoplegia.

3.q: What is the approximate latency of the vestibulo-ocular reflex?
3.e: The three-neuron arc (afferent → vestibular nucleus → oculomotor neuron) has a latency of about 10 ms, far faster than visual pursuit (about 100 ms).

3.q: Normal horizontal VOR gain (eye velocity ÷ head velocity) on the video head impulse test is closest to:
3.e: Normal gain is close to 1, so the eyes counter-rotate at head speed. Horizontal gains below about 0.8 with corrective saccades suggest a canal deficit.

3.q: On vHIT, impulses to the left give gain 0.98; impulses to the right give gain 0.40 with catch-up saccades. Where is the lesion?
o: Right horizontal canal or superior vestibular nerve
3.e: The deficit lies on the side toward which the head is turned. The right horizontal canal is supplied by the right superior vestibular nerve.

4.q: By convention, the direction of jerk nystagmus is named after:
o: The direction of gaze during testing
4.e: The slow phase is the pathological drift driven by the imbalance; the fast phase is the corrective reset, and it gives the nystagmus its name.

4.q: Which spontaneous nystagmus is expected in acute right vestibular neuritis?
o: Left-beating horizontal–torsional, stronger on left gaze, suppressed by fixation
Pure downbeat, not suppressed by fixation
4.e: Loss of right tone lets the left nuclei dominate: slow phase drifts right, fast phase beats left (toward the healthy ear). Peripheral nystagmus is reduced by fixation.

4.q: Alexander's law states that peripheral spontaneous nystagmus:
o: Is only visible with the eyes closed
Increases when gazing in the direction of the fast phase
Increases when gazing toward the slow phase
4.e: Peripheral nystagmus grows in amplitude when the patient looks toward the fast-phase direction and lessens looking the other way; it does not change direction.

4.q: Bithermal calorics show a 70 % right unilateral weakness (Jongkees formula). How is this interpreted?
o: Significant right canal paresis (above the 20–25 % cut-off)
4.e: Unilateral weakness above about 20–25 % is significant. Calorics test the horizontal canal and superior vestibular nerve at a very low frequency (≈ 0.003 Hz).

4.q: In Ménière's disease the caloric response is often reduced while vHIT gain is normal. What explains this dissociation?
o: The vHIT goggles slipped during testing
Hydrops affects the low-frequency caloric response more than the high-frequency head impulse
4.e: Calorics probe very low frequencies and vHIT high frequencies. A hydropic, enlarged duct can blunt the caloric convection response while preserving the impulse response.

5.q: Which semicircular canal is most commonly involved in BPPV?
5.e: The posterior canal accounts for about 85–90 % of BPPV because it is the most dependent part of the labyrinth when upright or supine, so debris settles there.

5.q: In a positive right Dix–Hallpike for right posterior-canal canalithiasis, the expected nystagmus is:
o: Horizontal, beating toward the uppermost ear
Upbeating–torsional, upper pole beating toward the left (upper) ear
Upbeating–torsional, upper pole beating toward the right (lower) ear
5.e: Ampullofugal flow excites the right posterior canal, producing upbeating torsional nystagmus with the upper pole beating toward the dependent (right) ear.

5.q: Which features best distinguish posterior-canal canalithiasis from central positional nystagmus?
o: Latency of a few seconds, duration under 60 s, fatigue on repetition
Immediate onset that persists as long as the position is held
Pure downbeat nystagmus with little vertigo
Nystagmus with marked truncal ataxia and other brainstem signs
5.e: Canalithiasis gives latency, a crescendo–decrescendo burst under 60 s, fatigability and reversal on sitting up. Persistent, pure vertical or atypical nystagmus suggests a central cause.

5.q: After the right Dix–Hallpike position, what is the next step of the Epley manoeuvre for right posterior-canal BPPV?
o: Roll onto the right side, nose down
Turn the head 90° to the left while keeping it extended
Flex the neck with the head turned 45° right
5.e: Epley: right Dix–Hallpike → head 90° left (still hanging) → roll onto the left side, nose down → sit up. Each position is held until nystagmus stops.

5.q: A 62-year-old has brief vertigo when rolling over in bed and a positive right Dix–Hallpike. What outcome can you counsel for the Epley manoeuvre?
o: Under 10 % improve; surgery is usually needed
About 80 % resolve after one to three manoeuvres
About 30 % improve and recurrence never occurs
5.e: Canalith repositioning succeeds in about 80 % after one to three manoeuvres. Recurrence is common over the years, so patients should know it can be repeated.

6.q: Per the Bárány Society (2015) criteria for definite Ménière's disease, spontaneous vertigo attacks last:
o: Under 1 minute, triggered by head position
5 minutes to 72 hours with migraine features
6.e: Definite MD: ≥ 2 spontaneous attacks of 20 min–12 h, audiometrically documented low-to-mid frequency SNHL in the affected ear, and fluctuating aural symptoms.

6.q: A patient has sound-induced vertigo, hears her own eye movements, and shows a low-frequency air–bone gap with supranormal bone conduction and present acoustic reflexes. Diagnosis?
6.e: A third-window lesion causes Tullio phenomenon, autophony and a pseudo-conductive gap. Present stapedial reflexes argue against otosclerosis; HRCT confirms the defect.

6.q: In acute vestibular syndrome, which HINTS finding points to a CENTRAL (stroke) cause?
o: Abnormal head impulse with a corrective saccade
Unidirectional horizontal nystagmus suppressed by fixation
6.e: INFARCT: Impulse Normal, Fast phase Alternating, Refixation on Cover Test (skew). Kattah (2009) found HINTS more sensitive than early MRI-DWI for stroke.

6.q: After IV gentamicin, a patient says the world 'jumps' when walking and balance is worse in the dark. Which symptom and diagnosis fit?
6.e: Bilateral loss abolishes the VOR, causing oscillopsia. Bárány criteria include bilateral vHIT gain < 0.6 or caloric response < 6°/s per side.

6.q: What is the most common cause of recurrent spontaneous (non-positional) episodic vertigo?
6.e: Vestibular migraine: episodes of 5 min–72 h with a migraine history and migraine features in at least half of episodes. Interictal tests are often normal.

7.q: After an acute unilateral vestibular loss, which process chiefly restores tonic balance between the vestibular nuclei?
o: Regeneration of hair cells in the crista
Regrowth of the damaged vestibular nerve
Central compensation via the cerebellum and commissural pathways
7.e: Human vestibular hair cells do not meaningfully regenerate. Recovery is central: the cerebellum and commissural fibres rebalance nuclear activity over days to weeks.

7.q: X1 gaze-stability exercises (fixating a stationary target while moving the head) work mainly through which mechanism?
7.e: Retinal slip during head movement is an error signal that drives adaptive increase of VOR gain. X2 (target and head moving opposite) is a harder progression.

7.q: Why should vestibular suppressants be limited to the first 1–3 days after acute vestibular neuritis?
o: They are toxic to the cochlea
7.e: Sedating suppressants (antihistamines, benzodiazepines) blunt the error signals the brain needs to compensate, so they are for acute nausea only.

7.q: Which rehabilitation strategy is emphasised for a patient with bilateral vestibulopathy?
o: Substitution with vision and proprioception, plus fall prevention
7.e: With little vestibular function left to adapt, therapy teaches reliance on visual and somatosensory cues, gaze strategies, and home and fall safety.

7.q: In unilateral Ménière's disease with vertigo not controlled by diet and betahistine, which intratympanic treatment is usually tried before gentamicin?
7.e: Non-destructive intratympanic steroid is tried first. Intratympanic gentamicin is ablative (chemical labyrinthectomy) and carries a risk to hearing.
